note.text: Air you breathe in through your nose or mouth goes down the windpipe, or trachea. Stiff rings keep it open.

steps.title: Bronchi
steps.instruction: Draw the two tubes branching to each lung.

note.text: The windpipe splits into two bronchi, one for each lung. Inside, they branch again and again into tiny tubes.

steps.title: Right lung
steps.instruction: Trace the lung on the left of the picture.

note.text: This is your right lung: the body faces you, so its right is on your left. It's the bigger lung.
note.remember: Two lungs, one on each side of the heart.

steps.title: Left lung
steps.instruction: Trace the other lung, with its dip in the middle.

note.text: The left lung is smaller. It has a dip, the cardiac notch, that makes room for your heart.
note.remember: The left lung makes room for the heart.

steps.title: Lobes
steps.instruction: Draw the two lines that split the right lung into lobes.

note.text: The right lung has three lobes, or sections. The left lung has two.

steps.title: Lobe
steps.instruction: Draw the line that splits the left lung into two lobes.

note.text: The lobes are separated by deep grooves called fissures.

steps.title: Air sacs
steps.instruction: Dab the tiny air sacs at the end of the airway.

note.text: The tiniest tubes end in air sacs called alveoli. Here oxygen passes into your blood, and carbon dioxide passes out to be breathed away.
note.remember: Alveoli: where oxygen enters the blood.

steps.title: Diaphragm
steps.instruction: Trace the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs.

note.text: The diaphragm is a muscle. When it squeezes, it moves down, making room in your chest, and air rushes into your lungs.

steps.title: Air's path
steps.instruction: Tap the parts in the order air reaches them.
steps.why: Air goes in through the nose or mouth, down the windpipe, into the bronchi, and on to the tiny air sacs.
steps.hint: Which tube does air go down first?

steps.title: Label the parts
steps.instruction: Pick the right name for each numbered part.

targets.role: Carries air down to the lungs.
Muscle that moves to pull air in.

mistakes.Stomach: The stomach is below the diaphragm. This dome-shaped muscle is the diaphragm.

commonMistakes.Heart: The heart sits between the lungs, in the dip of the left lung. It isn't drawn here.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: Why do your lungs need so many tiny air sacs?

options.text: So lots of oxygen can pass into the blood at once
options.feedback: Yes. Every air sac is a place where oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out, so more sacs means more oxygen.
Lungs don't store food. The air sacs are where oxygen gets into the blood.
The air sacs are about passing oxygen into the blood, not weight.
The heart pumps blood. The air sacs are where oxygen enters it.
